exclusion_rules: Exclude rows missing required raw or constructed variables.
Exclude nonpositive adjusted wages because log wage gain is undefined.

reference_specification.variable_construction: Compute log_wage_gain as log(lastUsWageAdjusted) - log(lastHomeWageAdjusted). Construct education groups from edyrs: <=8 no_high_school, 9-11 some_high_school, 12 high_school, 13-15 some_college, >=16 college_degree. Construct age_home_job as yearLastHomeJob - yrborn and age_home_job_sq as its square.

conclusion_rule.expected_direction: The no_high_school wage-gain coefficient relative to college_degree is positive.
conclusion_rule.statistical_threshold: p < 0.05 describes strong statistical evidence; p >= 0.05 with an expected-direction estimate remains weak directional support.
conclusion_rule.support_rule: Support when the focal point estimate or pattern is in the expected direction. Opposite requires affirmative evidence of a material effect in the contrary direction; an opposite-signed estimate alone is inconclusive. A non-significant result in the expected direction remains weak directional support.

evidence.paper: The focal claim appears on p. 682: immigrants who have never been to high school gain more on migration to the United States than immigrants with a college degree. The paper summary states that wage gains are calculated by comparing immigrants' pre- and post-migration hourly wages adjusted to U.S. dollars/PPP and that less educated workers have larger migration wage gains.
evidence.dataset_mapping: Verified columns edyrs, lastHomeWageAdjusted, lastUsWageAdjusted, country, sex, yrborn, yearLastHomeJob, and yearLastUsJob exist in data/wage_gain_table.xlsx. The dataset has 2854 rows and no missing values in these columns.

uncertainties: The exact original table/regression specification for p. 682 is not fully available from the summarized PDF text, so the OLS adjusted anchor uses verified variables and prior paper-described wage-gain construction.
The paper's exact standard-error method for this focal education comparison is not_stated in the readable summary.

analysis_path.path_description: Run Huber robust linear regression of individual log wage gain on education groups, using college degree as the reference and estimating the no-high-school contrast while adjusting for country, sex, age at last home job, squared age, and last home/U.S. job years.
preprocessing_steps: Load data/wage_gain_table.xlsx.
Verify required columns: edyrs, yearLastHomeJob, yearLastUsJob, sex, yrborn, lastHomeWageAdjusted, lastUsWageAdjusted, country.
Report starting rows.
Drop rows missing required raw columns and report removals.
Keep rows with lastHomeWageAdjusted > 0 and lastUsWageAdjusted > 0 and report removals.
Compute log_wage_gain = log(lastUsWageAdjusted) - log(lastHomeWageAdjusted).
Construct edu_group from edyrs with no_high_school <=8, some_high_school 9-11, high_school 12, some_college 13-15, college_degree >=16.
Construct age_home_job = yearLastHomeJob - yrborn and age_home_job_sq = age_home_job squared.
Drop rows with missing or nonfinite constructed variables and report removals.
Set college_degree as the education reference category and preserve intermediate education groups.
Fit robust linear model log_wage_gain on edu_group, country indicators, sex indicators, age_home_job, age_home_job_sq, yearLastHomeJob, and yearLastUsJob using HuberT weights.

Report the focal no_high_school versus college_degree coefficient, standard error, z statistic, p value, approximate 95% confidence interval, exponentiated percent difference, sample flow, and conclusion class.

candidates.decision_summary: Task1 passes all required checks. The original paper is observational and studies individual immigrants' wage gains from pre- to post-migration wages, including the focal statement that less educated immigrants, specifically those with no high-school exposure, gain more than college graduates. The authorized dataset is an individual-level wage-gain table with 2854 complete rows and verified columns for education, adjusted home and U.S. wages, country, sex, birth year, and job years. The code implements the declared Huber robust regression on log wage gain with college_degree as the reference education group, retains intermediate groups, uses verified controls, reports sample flow, and outputs the focal coefficient and inference quantities. The model deviates from the OLS anchor, but the deviation is explicit and methodologically justified by extreme wage values while preserving the focal outcome, contrast, sample, controls, and conclusion rule. No low-quality rule is triggered under M1-M6 or Task1 rules 1.1-1.9. Guardrails G1, G8, and G14 apply: a different defensible model from the paper/anchor and absence of additional diagnostics are not sufficient grounds for rejection. Verification limitation: I did not execute the code, consistent with pruning-agent restrictions.

The Task2 instruction requires the pooled poor-country NIS/Migration Projects sample including Mexico and prohibits sector agriculture/nonagriculture and rural/urban region controls. The authorized dataset contains 2854 individual rows, includes Mexico as the dominant country category, and has verified columns for education and adjusted wages. The code uses the supplied file with no country filter, constructs log wage gain and the no_high_school versus college_degree contrast, includes no controls, does not reference occupation/sector or region variables, reports sample flow, and outputs the focal coefficient and inference quantities. The use of Huber robust regression rather than the OLS anchor is an explicit, justified model-family deviation that preserves the Task2 outcome, contrast, sample, and control prohibition; therefore M1-M6 and Task2 rules 2.1-2.8 are not triggered. Guardrails G1, G8, and G14 apply because a defensible alternative model and absence of additional diagnostics are not by themselves low-quality.
